summary: Describes how to securely exchange structured business data, such as EDI, XML or other business-to-business data, over SMTP. The data is packaged as MIME content, with authentication and privacy provided by cryptographic means. This is the basis of the AS1 style of exchange.

plainLanguage.summary: This document describes how two companies can exchange order or invoice data by email and both end up with proof of what happened. The data is packed into standard email formats, encrypted and signed, and the receiver can be asked to send back a signed receipt that carries a fingerprint of what it received.

subtitle: How to send structured business data over email with encryption, a digital signature and a signed receipt.

tldr.problem: Business data such as EDI, XML or other trading documents has to travel over the Internet between trading partners, and both sides need proof of who sent it, that nobody read it, and that it arrived.
tldr.mechanism: The data is packaged with standard MIME content types and secured with S/MIME or PGP/MIME security multiparts. A sender can request a signed receipt, which the receiver returns as a multipart/signed message disposition notification carrying the Received-content-MIC of the message it received.
tldr.outcome: Together these give the four properties the RFC names: data privacy, data integrity and authenticity, non-repudiation of origin and non-repudiation of receipt. The document is written as an applicability statement that combines existing RFCs rather than defining a new protocol.

today: RFC 3335 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2002. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What This Document Adds
sections.content:
Earlier work on Internet EDI focused on specifying MIME content types for EDI data in RFC 1767. This document expands on RFC 1767 to specify use of a comprehensive set of data security features: data privacy, data integrity and authenticity, non-repudiation of origin, and non-repudiation of receipt. While the document focuses specifically on EDI data, any other data type is also supported.

The RFC lists the specifications it builds on: RFC 821 SMTP, RFC 822 text message formats, RFC 1767 EDI content type, RFC 1847 security multiparts for MIME, RFC 1892 multipart/report, RFC 2015, 3156 and 2440 for PGP/MIME, RFC 2045 to 2049 for MIME, RFC 2298 message disposition notification, and RFC 2630 and 2633 for S/MIME version 3.

The stated intent is to define clearly and precisely how these are used together, and what is required by user agents to be compliant. It also recognizes contemporary RFCs and tries to re-invent as little as possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here is a new protocol. It is a rulebook for using existing email standards together in one order, so that two programs on either side of a trade agree on what to send.

sections.title: Receipts and the Secure Transmission Loop
sections.content:
The purpose of these specifications is to ensure interoperability between EDI user agents invoking some or all of the commonly expected security features. The document is not limited to strict EDI use, but applies to any electronic commerce application where business data needs to be exchanged over the Internet in a secure manner.

The terms are defined as follows. A receipt is the functional message sent from a receiver to a sender to acknowledge receipt of an interchange, and a signed receipt is the same with a digital signature. A message disposition notification is the Internet messaging format used to convey a receipt, and the terms are used interchangeably. Non-repudiation of receipt is a legal event that occurs when the original sender has verified the signed receipt coming back from the receiver; it is not a functional or technical message.

The secure transmission loop has three steps. The sending organization signs and encrypts the data using either PGP/MIME or S/MIME, and the message requests a signed receipt. The receiving organization decrypts the message and verifies the signature, which gives verified integrity of the data and authenticity of the sender. The receiving organization then returns a signed receipt in the form of a message disposition notification, and that signed receipt contains the hash of the signature from the received message.

The document assumes that a typical EDI interchange is the lowest level object subject to security services: in ANSI X12 anything between and including the segments ISA and IEA, and in EDIFACT anything between and including the segments UNA/UNB and UNZ. The envelope headers are therefore not visible in the MIME package. The RFC does not dictate the use or non-use of the X12.58 and AUTACK security standards, which are compatible with it.

Eight permutations are possible in a trading relationship: the sender may send unencrypted, signed, encrypted, or encrypted and signed data, and with or without a receipt request. Only the last one, encrypted and signed data with a signed receipt requested, offers the whole suite of security features.
sections.plainLanguage: A receipt is a message back saying the data arrived. A signed receipt carries a signature, so the sender can show the receiver really sent it. Full protection needs all three pieces: encrypted data, a signature on it, and a signed receipt coming back.

sections.title: How the Message Is Wrapped
sections.content:
The structures are described hierarchically in terms of which RFCs are applied to form the specific structure, and they describe the initial transmission only; receipts are handled separately. With PGP/MIME, a message with no encryption and no signature is an RFC 822 and 2045 message containing an RFC 1767 body of type application/EDIxxxx or /xml. Adding a signature wraps that body in an RFC 1847 multipart/signed with an application/pgp-signature part. Adding encryption instead wraps it in an RFC 1847 multipart/encrypted holding an application/pgp-encrypted part with the text Version: 1 and an application/octet-stream part that carries the encrypted RFC 1767 body. Encryption and signature together nest the multipart/signed inside the encrypted part.

With S/MIME the same four cases are expressed with different content types. No encryption and no signature is an RFC 822 and 2045 message with an RFC 1767 body. A signature is an RFC 1847 multipart/signed holding the RFC 1767 body and an RFC 2633 application/pkcs7-signature part. Encryption without a signature is an RFC 2633 application/pkcs7-mime holding the encrypted RFC 1767 body. Encryption with a signature is an RFC 2633 application/pkcs7-mime holding an RFC 1847 multipart/signed in which both the RFC 1767 body and the RFC 2633 application/pkcs7-signature are encrypted.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to wrap the data, S/MIME or PGP/MIME, and four ways to combine them: plain, signed, encrypted, or both. Each combination has a fixed set of nested MIME parts, so a receiver knows where to find the data.

sections.title: Requesting and Returning a Signed Receipt
sections.content:
To support non-repudiation of receipt, a signed receipt is implemented by a receiving trading partner's user agent. The message disposition notification specified by RFC 2298 is digitally signed by the receiving partner as part of a multipart/signed MIME message.

Support for signed receipts requires the ability to create a multipart/report whose report-type is disposition-notification, to calculate a message integrity check on the received message and return that value inside the signed receipt, to create a multipart/signed content with the notification as the first body part and the signature as the second, and to return the signed receipt to the sending partner.

The receiver decrypts the symmetric key and initialization vector with its private key, decrypts the interchange with that key, and then authenticates the signature using the sender's public key: the message integrity check is decrypted with the sender's public key, a message integrity check over the signed contents is calculated with the same one-way hash function, and the two are compared. The receiver then formats the notification and sets the calculated MIC into the Received-content-MIC extension field, and creates a multipart/signed message in which the notification is the first part and the signature is created over it, including its MIME headers. The protocol option is application/pkcs-7-signature for S/MIME and application/pgp-signature for PGP/MIME.

A receipt is requested by placing a Disposition-notification-to header in the message, holding the return address for the notification. A signed receipt is requested by following it with a Disposition-Notification-Options header whose parameters are attribute, equals sign, importance and values, where the importance is required or optional. The two parameters signed-receipt-protocol and signed-receipt-micalg are both required when requesting a signed receipt. The supported protocol symbols are pkcs7-signature and pgp-signature, and the supported MIC algorithms are md5 and sha1.

The RFC gives three rules for receipts. If a receipt is requested with an explicit request that it be signed, the receipt MUST be returned with a signature. If the recipient cannot support the requested protocol format or the requested MIC algorithms, then either a signed or an unsigned receipt SHOULD be returned. If a signature is not explicitly requested, or the signed receipt request parameter is not recognized, then no receipt, an unsigned receipt or a signed receipt MAY be returned. When a request for a signed receipt is made but there is an error in processing the contents, a signed receipt MUST still be returned, with the reason set in the disposition field.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender asks for a receipt with two email headers. The receiver decrypts the message, checks the signature, and sends back a signed notice carrying a hash of what it received. Even when something goes wrong, the signed receipt still has to be sent back, with the reason recorded in it.

sections.title: The Notification Format and the MIC Field
sections.content:
The format of a message disposition notification is specified in RFC 2298, and this document names the fields used for Internet EDI: content-type, reporting-ua-field, MDN-gateway-field, original-recipient-field, final-recipient-field, original-message-id-field, and the disposition-field.

Three groups of disposition values are recommended. The disposition-mode values are automatic-action, meaning the disposition resulted from an automatic action rather than an explicit instruction by the user, and manual-action. The second part of the mode is MDN-sent-automatically, meaning the user agent had previously been configured to send the notification, or MDN-sent-manually, meaning the user gave explicit permission for this particular notification. The disposition-type values are processed, meaning the message was processed in some manner such as printing, faxing, forwarding or gatewaying without being displayed to the user, and failed, meaning a failure prevented the proper generation of a notification. The disposition-modifier values are error, meaning an error prevented successful processing, and warning, meaning the message was processed but an exceptional condition occurred.

The Received-content-MIC extension field is added after the disposition field to support signed receipts. It is set when the integrity of the received message is verified. The MIC is the base64 encoded quantity computed over the received message with a hash function, and the algorithm used must be the same as the micalg value used by the sender in the multipart/signed message. When no signature is received, or the micalg parameter is not supported, it is RECOMMENDED that SHA1 be used.

For a signed message the returned MIC is calculated on the RFC 1767 MIME header and content, with canonicalization as specified in RFC 1848 performed first. For an encrypted unsigned message it is calculated on the decrypted RFC 1767 MIME header and content, which must also be canonicalized. For an unsigned unencrypted message the MIC is calculated over the message contents prior to Content-Transfer-Encoding and without the MIME or any other RFC 822 headers, because those are sometimes altered or reordered by mail transfer agents.
sections.plainLanguage: The receipt carries one extra field: a hash of the message the receiver got, plus the name of the hash function. The sender compares it with its own copy, and that comparison is what proves the message arrived unchanged.

sections.title: Public Key Certificate Handling
sections.content:
In the near term, the exchange of public keys and certification of these keys must be handled as part of the process of establishing a trading partnership. The user agent and the EDI application interface must maintain a database of public keys used for encryption or signatures, in addition to the mapping between EDI trading partner ID and RFC 822 email address.

For systems that make use of X.509 certificates, it is RECOMMENDED that trading partners self-certify each other if an agreed certification authority is not used. It is highly RECOMMENDED that trading partners using S/MIME also exchange public key certificates using the recommendations in the S/MIME Version 3 Message Specification. This applicability statement does not require the use of a certification authority, so its use is OPTIONAL.

In the long term, additional Internet-EDI standards may be developed to simplify establishing a trading partnership, including third party authentication of trading partners and attributes of the trading relationship.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides need each other's public key before anything can be signed. The document says to handle that as part of setting up the trading relationship, and it does not insist on a certificate authority.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The entire document is concerned with secure transport of business to business data, and considers both privacy and authentication issues.

On cryptography, the document quotes the S/MIME Version 2 Message Specification: 40-bit encryption is considered weak by most cryptographers, and using weak cryptography offers little actual security over sending plain text. However, other features of S/MIME, such as the specification of tripleDES or AES and the ability to announce stronger cryptographic capabilities to parties with whom you communicate, allow senders to create messages that use strong encryption. Using weak cryptography is never recommended unless the only alternative is no cryptography.

On certificates, the document quotes the S/MIME Version 2 Certificate Handling: certificate processing may fail in many situations, and if a certificate is not provably valid and associated with the message, the processing software should take immediate and noticeable steps to inform the end user. The listed failures are that no certificate chain leads to a trusted CA, no ability to check the CRL for a certificate, an invalid CRL was received, the CRL being checked is expired, the certificate is expired, and the certificate has been revoked.
sections.plainLanguage: Weak encryption is no better than no encryption. And when a certificate cannot be checked, the program must tell the user plainly rather than carry on silently.
